articles.body: Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday for the first time since Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack, in a closely contested election seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The vote follows three years of regional wars, with Netanyahu running neck and neck with centrist rival Gadi Eisenkot.
articles.headline: Israel votes in first election since October 7 attack as Netanyahu faces crucial test

articles.body: French football star Kylian Mbappe was dropped by two major Chinese brands on Tuesday after a video circulated online in which he appeared to joke about former leader Mao Zedong. Energy drink giant Dongpeng and dairy producer Mengniu said they had terminated their partnerships, citing remarks that offended Chinese national sentiment.
articles.headline: Kylian Mbappe loses two major China sponsorship deals over Mao Zedong joke

articles.body: US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer warned on Monday that a $3.4 billion European Investment Bank loan to Airbus could jeopardise a tariff truce between Washington and Brussels. Greer said his office had received no details about the financing, announced in June, and urged the EU to resolve the matter quickly.
articles.headline: US-EU trade truce at risk over $3.4 billion Airbus loan, Trump official warns

articles.body: Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro said on Monday a Supreme Court justice had barred him from leaving the country after he narrowly lost to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro, who refused to concede defeat, denounced the order as intimidation and vowed to challenge the election results.
articles.headline: Flavio Bolsonaro vows to lead opposition after Brazil court imposes travel ban

articles.body: Harry Kane became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the Ballon d’Or on Monday after scoring 73 goals for club and country last season. Spain’s Alexia Putellas claimed her third women’s award after helping Barcelona win the Champions League, ending teammate Aitana Bonmati’s three-year reign.
articles.headline: Harry Kane ends England's 25-year Ballon d'Or drought, Putellas wins third crown

articles.body: Europe's five main NATO members said on Monday they were ready to take greater responsibility for the continent's security while reaffirming the United States as an "indispensable ally". Defence ministers from France, Germany, Italy, Poland and Britain pledged closer co-operation with Washington after talks in Paris on strengthening Europe's defence role.
articles.headline: Europe's top NATO powers pledge greater defence role, reaffirm US alliance

articles.body: Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks in Iran on Monday aimed at preventing renewed fighting in the Middle East, with Tehran describing discussions as “very good”. The diplomatic push, attended by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, followed warnings from Washington, Tehran and Israel of renewed hostilities.
articles.headline: Mecca pact nations hold talks with Iran to prevent renewed Middle East war

articles.body: As young people protest poor school conditions and the rising cost of living across Europe, misleading videos are spreading online. Footage from Poland in 2017, military preparations in Portugal and a protest in Argentina have all been falsely presented as recent demonstrations in Europe, painting a misleading picture of unrest. Vedika Bahl fact-checks three viral videos to uncover what they really show and how old footage is recycled to spread misinformation and attract clicks.
articles.headline: Protests in Europe: Fact-checking viral videos amid claims of 'chaos'

articles.body: AI giant Anthropic has publicly filed for an initial public offering (IPO) with US market regulators. The document offered a glimpse into the company's finances but also contained nearly 100 pages related to risks around investing in the company. The filing revealed that in the first half of 2026, its revenue soared to $16.3 billion while net loss widened to over $80 billion. Plus, London's iconic Oxford Street, one of Europe's busiest shopping areas, has been partially pedestrianised.
articles.headline: Anthropic's IPO filing shows soaring sales and steep losses

articles.body: On October 25, Serbia's student-led protest movement won a historic victory in parliamentary ⁠elections, defeating outgoing President Aleksandar Vucic's party. Supporters of the student list explained to FRANCE 24 how they mounted a massive mobilisation to fight electoral fraud and monitor the electoral process inside and outside the polling stations.
articles.headline: Serbia’s elections: 'Tracking fraud for sure had an impact on the results'

articles.body: In tonight's edition, 15 military officials are sanctioned by the UK over the brutality and abuse of civilians during the fall of El Fasher. Also, ⁠Algeria's set to send in army units ​to ‌Niger ⁠to ‌protect energy ⁠and economic interests there. And days after a foreigner was beaten to death on the streets of Durban, the stalled asylum process has left many migrants living in fear.
articles.headline: The fall of El-Fasher, one year on

articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Monday pledged a $1 million reward for information on voter fraud leading to conviction ahead of the upcoming 2026 US midterms on November 3. The president gave no details of how the reward would be funded or administered. The comments follow his repeated false claims that he won the 2020 presidential election.
articles.headline: Trump offers $1 million for tipoffs leading to vote fraud conviction as midterms approach

articles.body: Emotions ran high in Belgrade on Monday after a student-led movement upset the right-wing populist Aleksandar Vucic's party in Serbia's snap election. A celebratory mood gripped the capital, with drivers honking their horns and passers-by holding up three fingers -- the winning list's ballot number and a Serbian greeting. Many wore badges and other symbols of the student movement, while a large group of residents spent the day cleaning up a park between parliament and the presidency after Vucic loyalists, who had camped there for more than a year, fled. FRANCE 24's Mark Owen speaks with researchers and political activist Aleksandar Matković.
articles.headline: Serbian student movement eyes power after election triumph

articles.body: Two days shy of his 81st birthday… Brazil’s Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva emerging as the comeback kid. Coming from behind in the polls after a bitter campaign where he often showed his age, Lula becoming the first candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s to win the presidential runoff after trailing in the first round. How did the Workers Party leader turn a 2-point-2 million vote deficit against the far-right's Flavio Bolsonaro into a 4-point-4 million vote win? Reminder that three short weeks ago, most races at the federal and state level broke the way of conservatives and the far-right?
articles.headline: Comeback kid: How did Brazil veteran-leader Lula upset Bolsonaro?

articles.body: The United Nations on Monday raised "ethnic cleansing" concerns following Israel's operation to displace by force more than 3,000 Palestinians from their homes in Hebron in the West Bank after two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint near the city on Friday. UN rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement that the "aggressive operation" must end, and that "collective punishment is a grave violation of international law".
articles.headline: UN cites 'ethnic cleansing' concerns around Israel's Palestinian displacement operation in Hebron

articles.body: The French government met student representatives on Monday (October 26) following weeks of unrest. Students who had been demanding a meeting for weeks hail progress. Nonetheless they are now calling for fresh demonstrations next Saturday (October 31) to press for further measures. Details by FRANCE 24’s French Politics Editor Marc Perelman.
articles.headline: French student union leaders call for 'continued mobilisation' after meeting PM

articles.body: Climate activists in Brazil are celebrating President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's election victory as good news for the Amazon rainforest. His last four years in power saw a record decrease in deforestation in the world's largest rainforest.
articles.headline: Brazil: What does Lula's re-election mean for the Amazon?

articles.body: Israel's defence minister denied on Monday (October 26) reports of a rift between PM Netanyahu and the army over Iran, before the vote. Netanyahu has campaigned heavily on his security credentials, insisting only he can "finish the job" in the US-Israeli war on Iran. His main rival, ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, has accused him of playing up the Iran threat when it suits him politically, and of failing to accomplish his war goals. FRANCE 24's Kethevane Gorjestani tells us more.
articles.headline: Opponents accuse Netanyahu of stoking tensions with Iran before Israel's election

articles.body: ​President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won Brazil's presidential election on Sunday (October 25), defeating right-wing ​Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in a runoff to secure a fourth non-consecutive term.
articles.headline: Leaders across Americas react to Brazil President Lula's re-election

articles.body: Israeli presidential candidate Gadi Eisenkot's pledge made Sunday to "heal" Israeli society after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's divisive tenure resonated with some voters attending his final campaign rally before polling begins Tuesday. Netanyahu meanwhile received fresh backing for re-election from US President Donald Trump and deemed Eisenkot "soft" on Iran.
articles.headline: Israeli candidate Eisenkot pledges to unite country as Netanyahu deems him 'soft' on Iran

articles.body: Erin Ogunkeye is pleased to welcome Christopher Sabatini, Director of Chatham House's Latin America Programme. Sabatini examines how Lula's campaign reinvention, youth mobilisation, and the changing dynamics of Bolsonarismo are reshaping Brazil's political landscape. By embracing social media, mobilising younger voters, and shifting attention from his historical achievements to the economic anxieties of ordinary Brazilians, Lula managed to transform the electoral contest. As Sabatini explains, voters were no longer satisfied with hearing about the past. They wanted an answer to a more immediate question: "What are you going to do for us now?
articles.headline: 'Lula accustomed to negotiating tough bargains': Campaign promises collide with right-wing Congress

articles.body: Israelis can’t vote from abroad, so tens of thousands of expats are expected to fly home for the election. At Tel Aviv airport, supporters of opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot are already waiting at arrivals. A “Fly and Vote” initiative helps expats organise their trip, despite a failed petition from Netanyahu’s Likud party to restrict it. With polls predicting a tight race, every vote could count, and the result will decide the Prime Minister’s fate.
articles.headline: Israel election: unable to vote from abroad, expats have to fly home

articles.headline: Macklemore holds charity stadium shows to raise funds for Palestine

articles.body: The French government sought to draw a line Monday under weeks of protests that have been marred by violence, with President Emmanuel Macron heading to Marseille. France has been rocked by widespread anger over the rising cost of living, with nationwide demonstrations on October 17 degenerating into some of the country's worst rioting in years.
articles.headline: France protests: Macron rules out state of emergency – for now

articles.body: 🚨🚨MUST READ🚨🚨: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and a group of fellow basketball enthusiasts have been secretly using the NYPD Police Academy’s gymnasium in Queens to play pickup ball, according to four people familiar with the games. The mayor and his crew typically show up around 10 or 11 p.m. and enter surreptitiously through a loading dock before hitting the court. While sports fanaticism has often buoyed the political brand of past mayors, Mamdani’s choice of venue is raising eyebrows. Read the story from POLITICO’s Graham Rayman, Chris Sommerfeldt and Joe Anuta here . FINANCE FLAWS: Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman’s campaign finance disclosure reports have been plagued by inaccuracies since the spring. Copies of the campaign’s bank statements obtained by POLITICO suggest his filings might have even more problems than previously suspected. According to a disclosure report submitted to the state Board of Elections earlier this month, the Blakeman campaign had only $178,000 in the bank as of Sept. 28. Yet the campaign’s checking account had a balance of $1.7 million on Sept. 28, according to TD Bank’s monthly statement. The bank records also show dozens of transactions that are missing from his campaign finance filings. On July 29, for example, the bank statements identified the campaign using a check with the number 1156 to make a $13,500 payment to an unspecified recipient. Yet Blakeman’s campaign finance reports do not identify any transactions that used check number 1156. It also hasn’t shown a single payment totaling $13,500 at any point over the past year. In addition, there are instances in which the bank records show apparent contributions to the campaign that never show up in the disclosure reports. The statements show Blakeman was wired $18,000 by actress Lois Robbins on Sept. 2, for example, while the filings don’t show any transactions totaling $18,000 within two weeks of that date or any donations from Robbins. An $18,000 wire from attorney and campaign finance chair Howard Fensterman in July similarly doesn’t match anything in the disclosure reports. Blakeman is the first gubernatorial candidate in state history to participate in the new matching funds program that lets him receive up to $3.5 million in public money. Then-Mayor Eric Adams was blocked from participating in a similar New York City program last year due to discrepancies between his bank statements and disclosure reports. Reinvent Albany’s Kyle Kennedy said he didn’t know the cause of the discrepancies, but that it could just be due to “the timing of when things were recorded.” But, he noted, Blakeman’s campaign “will automatically be audited by the Board of Elections after the election. … Campaign finance enforcement takes place after elections, not in real-time.” Blakeman’s campaign didn’t respond to a request to explain the discrepancies. It has previously said its campaign finance problems are due to technical issues caused by a large number of donors. Several of the candidate’s campaign finance disclosure reports have been repeatedly amended, often in ways that made the initial numbers wildly inaccurate. His July report showed him with $4.7 million in the bank; that was changed a week later to show his balance was $6.1 million; then in August it was changed to $4.3 million. As POLITICO reported earlier this month , Blakeman has received about $360,000 in donations over the contribution limit that he still needs to return. Many of the donations he has already returned have been highly unusual — one person who gave $1 in July was quickly refunded $780.76. His campaign then said he accidentally submitted some duplicate contributions. Nearly a month later, it hasn’t amended the filing to show which transactions were real. And as New York Focus reported , the Blakeman campaign submitted requests to receive matching funds for 2,600 donations that were ineligible for matches. From the Capitol THE WEEKEND TURNOUT: Early voting turnout has skyrocketed in every corner of the state, according to unofficial tallies provided by the state Board of Elections. On the first two days of early voting in 2022, 261,735 people cast a ballot. This weekend, that number increased to 485,205 — a jump of roughly 85 percent. The biggest increases were in the North Country — particularly in the congressional seat being vacated by Rep. Elise Stefanik, which is now a battleground district for the first time in over a decade. Washington County’s weekend turnout was up 236 percent from four years ago. Early voting increased 196 percent in St. Lawrence County, 182 percent in Warren County, and 179 percent in Herkimer County. The smallest gains were in the Hudson Valley. That was especially true in the district held by Democratic Rep. Pat Ryan, where early turnout was the highest in the state four years ago as Ryan won his first full term in a nail-biter. His race isn’t widely viewed as competitive this year, and the smallest increase among the state’s 62 counties was in Ulster, which was up only 41 percent relative to 2022. There were also relatively middling gains in Erie County (up 60 percent) and Nassau County (up 64 percent). Those are the places where New York’s two gubernatorial candidates live, perhaps indicating that neither is yet the beneficiary of any outpourings of hometown pride. — Bill Mahoney FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL ORDER’S UP: Republican Rep. Mike Lawler spent part of this afternoon working at McDonald’s in Haverstraw – a potential backup job “if things don’t work out in November,” he said while putting on his uniform. Lawler is in the final campaign stretch in one of the country’s most closely watched congressional battlegrounds against Democrat Cait Conley. The lawmaker spent his McDonald’s shift cooking food, handing out orders and speaking with constituents – one of whom openly admitted to voting against him before taking their food and driving off. Aside from that one outlier, customers gave Lawler a warm reception at the drive-thru window. The visit was seemingly part of an effort to make inroads in Haverstraw, a town that leans Democratic. Lawler told POLITICO he’s feeling confident going into the final days of his campaign, but insisted that he is an underdog in the Hudson Valley district. In the 2024 presidential election, Kamala Harris and Lawler each won the district. “I feel very good about where we are heading on Election Day. Eight days from now, we’re going to win because I’ve done the work,” Lawler said in an interview. “I’ve delivered for my district, and the people here know me. I’m from here; I’ve lived here my whole life, I know the community..” And for those wondering about Lawler’s go-to McDonald’s order: double quarter-pounder with cheese, a Coke and a four-piece McNugget. — Katelyn Cordero STUMPING SPRINT: Fresh off a weekend of enthusiastic campaigning for Gov. Kathy Hochul , the mayor addressed reporters at a press conference this morning. He stuck to his rhetoric touting the governor as a champion for affordable child care and lampooning her GOP foe Bruce Blakeman as a Trump puppet. The mayor was also pressed about whether he expects something in return for all the campaigning he’s been doing for Hochul — such as increased taxes on the rich, a top goal for Mamdani and his democratic socialist allies in the state Legislature. “I’m expecting a continuation of a positive and productive working relationship with the governor,” he said. “I’m excited for that relationship to continue. It’s been one that’s delivered for working class New Yorkers, and I’m confident it’s going to keep delivering.” It’s far from an explicit commitment, but it suggests he’ll continue pushing Hochul for tax hikes should she win reelection — something City Council Speaker Julie Menin told POLITICO she would support to bankroll child care programs earlier this month. Mamdani also repeatedly mentioned the importance of showing New Yorkers that a mayor and a governor can have a productive working relationship — an apparent dig at the storied feud between former Mayor Bill de Blasio and former Governor Andrew Cuomo . “New Yorkers across the five boroughs are excited about us finally working together, where they haven’t seen mayors and governors do that often in the past to be able to deliver on common sense things,” he said. — Molly Reinmann FROM CITY HALL GRAND PLANS: Mamdani’s chief of staff Elle Bisgaard-Church laid out the democratic socialist administration’s governing philosophy today — including its opposition to means-testing for government programs. “We look especially to universal social programs, facilitating forms of collective ownership, supporting the growth of unions. In short, creating shared economic security and stability through material programs,” Bisgaard-Church said at an event on Mamdani’s affordability agenda hosted by the New York City Policy Forum, a left-leaning research and publishing network. “On the contrary, means-tested programs segregate and encumber people.” She pointed to other periods in the city’s history that saw “rich public institutions that could compete with the private sector,” citing NYCHA, the MTA and CUNY. Public housing, in particular, has seen significant deterioration in recent decades amid federal disinvestment. Reversing that trajectory is one of the most pressing issues Mamdani faces as mayor. “Today we are governed by rules of austerity and face a withered welfare regime, means-tested policies, decayed public sector, and weakened public institutions,” Bisgaard-Church continued. “These are the political realities our administration wants to overturn, and we know that tackling the crushing cost of living is again key to doing so.” The event drew other top Mamdani officials including Deputy Mayor for Housing and Planning Leila Bozorg, Economic Development Corporation Chair Lina Khan, and Consumer and Worker Protection Commissioner Sam Levine. — Janaki Chadha IN OTHER NEWS — HOMELESSNESS: Mamdani’s early efforts to address a ballooning homelessness problem in the city have largely failed, community leaders allege. ( The Wall Street Journal ) — SUNNYSIDE YARD: Housing experts weighed in on the outlandishly high cost of Mamdani and Trump’s proposed development at Sunnyside Yard. ( The City Reporter ) — BK DEMS: There are four state legislative seats Democrats are looking to flip in southern Brooklyn this midterm cycle, a fact that has largely been overshadowed by the party’s drama-packed leadership succession saga. articles.body: House Democrats are pushing into redder and redder territory. History shows those last-minute moves don’t usually pan out, even in favorable cycles. Since 2018, Democrats haven’t flipped any Republican-held seat that was added to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s “Red to Blue” list in the September or October before Election Day, according to a POLITICO analysis. Of the 28 total candidates from 2018 to 2024 that were added in the final two months of the campaign, just three Democrats won — all in Democratic-held open seats. That’s a much lower rate than average Red to Blue performance. Out of 203 candidates added to the program in the four previous cycles, 73 flipped their seats. That’s not a shock: The DCCC tends to add the biggest reaches later as it moves through the cycle, both to make sure its best opportunities are funded first and have enough attention and to try to create a sense of momentum and map expansion for donors and the media. In fact, the DCCC used some of the seats in their latest round of additions in a recent fundraising plea sent out by Executive Director Julie Merz, who warned that without more cash the committee “could be leaving winnable races on the table.” But it illuminates how hard it is — even in the best of environments — to reach deep into red territory in order to flip House seats. And it’s especially true now, as the House battlefield has shrunk significantly since 2018 because of gerrymandering. Since the beginning of September, the DCCC has added nine Democrats to Red to Blue: independent Bill Hill in AK-AL; Will Lawrence in MI-07; Mitchell Berman in WI-01; Chris Jones in AR-02; Dwayne Romero in CO-03; Eliott Rodriguez in FL-27; Teresa Benitez-Thompson in NV-02; Blake Gendebien in NY-21; and Justin Pearson in TN-09. Democrats acknowledge these late additions are a low-percentage play. Former DCCC staffer Cole Leiter, who worked there for the 2018 and 2020 cycles, said the committee recruits and tracks reach-district candidates early in the cycle with hopes the political winds will shift their way. “That is an investment in the unpredictability of the map,” Leiter said. “Most of these seats probably won’t flip, but one or two might.” Regardless of whether or not Democrats ultimately win the seats they’ve added late this year (the DCCC added six deep-red targets to Red to Blue in early October) — the additions alone contribute to a narrative of a party on offense. And they can also be a boon for fundraising for those specific candidates as well as to entice donors with exactly which areas their dollars will go if they pony up. “Even if there's ultimately not a massive success rate in those final editions, it is not a bad thing to make sure that those campaigns have any last-minute dollars that the designation can bring,” said Meredith Kelly, a former DCCC staffer who worked the 2016 and 2018 cycles. “Just make sure that they have a surfboard in the water and have an ability to potentially take advantage of a really, really good night.” This cycle’s late-add Democrats are almost all facing cash disadvantages against their incumbent GOP opponents. Of the nine Democrats added within the past two months, only one — Benitez-Thompson, running against Republican David Flippo — has reported more cash on hand than their opponent. Five of them are facing fundraising deficits of over $1 million, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Democrats’ poor record in these seats is somewhat self-selecting — seats added to the program late in the cycle reflect the fact that Democrats weren’t initially convinced they could be flipped. Whitney Fox, who lost by 9 points to GOP Rep. Anna Paulina Luna in FL-13 in 2024 and was among the last Democrats to be added to Red to Blue when she was picked in late September, said her campaign suffered from the delay in adding her to the program, even as she acknowledged the DCCC is forced to make strategic decisions with limited resources. The late additions also limit the window that candidates can capitalize on the program’s benefits. After initially being told she wouldn’t be added and after what she said was months of making her case to the DCCC, Fox made the list just before Hurricane Milton devastated the Tampa area, which she said made it difficult to fundraise off her newly minted Red to Blue status. “I felt like it was too little, too late,” she said. The Democrat running against Luna this cycle, Leela Gray, was added to Red to Blue in late August. Fox, who is informally advising local Florida candidates this cycle, said she offered Gray advice on how to make the list early. “I was a squeaky wheel trying to talk to leadership and Democratic members of Congress, and then it got to a certain point where I was no longer the squeaky wheel,” she said she relayed to Gray. “I was going to take the spoke off the wheel and hit people over the head with it.” Still the DCCC believes this cycle will be different, history be damned. And if recent national polling showing them with a double-digit lead in the generic ballot is correct, some of these late additions might break through. “Records are meant to be broken,” DCCC spokesperson Viet Shelton said in a statement. “We’re on track to break them this year because across the battlefield, we’ve got amazing recruits and the enthusiasm to fire House Republicans for making life unaffordable is off the charts.” A version of this article first appeared in POLITICO Pro’s Morning Score. articles.body: Republicans spurned by President Donald Trump aren't interested in rescuing their would-be replacements. Instead, a growing number of retiring or ousted GOP incumbents from Nevada to North Carolina are sitting those races out, and in some cases, openly bucking their own party. Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn has raised money for various Republican Senate candidates — just not for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who ousted him in the primary with support from Trump. He’s been vocal for months about what he sees as Paxton’s vulnerabilities and how Democrats could flip Texas blue for the first time in decades. North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis — who has frequently criticized some of Trump’s Cabinet and broken with the White House on policy — has played little role in the campaign of former RNC Chair Michael Whatley, Trump’s hand-picked Senate candidate. The distance between the two Republicans is particularly notable as Whatley struggles to close the gap against Democrat Roy Cooper. Rep. Mark Amodei has repeatedly criticized, and now openly rejected voting for , the GOP nominee to replace him, David Flippo. “The bedwetting from outgoing moderate Republicans will define their legacy and only help socialists get elected,” said David McIntosh, president of the Trump-aligned Club for Growth, which has endorsed Flippo and Paxton. “People like John Cornyn and Mark Amodei need to get on board and support Republican nominees and stop posturing for an MSNOW contract.” But other Republicans defended their colleagues: “I never would question the loyalty to the party of Thom Tillis or John Cornyn. Both of them have contributed immensely to our party and our party's successes in the past and I suspect will be going forward,” said North Dakota GOP Sen. Kevin Cramer. “But I also don't begrudge them for their opinions and their right to be open about them.” These outgoing Republicans, several of whom were explicitly pushed out by Trump or persuaded to retire given his hold on the GOP, are using the midterms as a test: whether the party will demand loyalty to the president or can return to a pre-Trump era. “What [Trump’s] done is created a coalition that, in my opinion, will not stay with Republicans once we go back to traditional Republican platform priorities,” Tillis said in a recent interview with POLITICO . “A lot of the elements of the populism that Trump created to expand a base that made him successful running for president, I don't think that stays with the party long-term.” Some of those intraparty frustrations are starting to boil over, with Trump loyalist candidates and outgoing Republicans swiping at one another as Election Day barrels closer and the party’s overall fortunes look dire. The blame game is especially prominent in some of the Senate battlegrounds where Republicans have begun to quietly retreat in the final stretch of the midterms. Tillis never followed through on his offers to help Whatley by reaching out to holdout donors in the North Carolina Senate race, said one person familiar with the campaign who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about internal matters. "He was never part of our strategy because ... I mean, if he could have been helpful to us, then he could have ran," the person said, referring to Tillis' decision not to seek reelection last year. "The Tillis of the past year ain’t the same guy who worked overtime to help elect Republican majorities here in NC back in 2010." One person with knowledge of Tillis and North Carolina politics, also granted anonymity to speak candidly, countered that the outgoing GOP senator “doesn’t help sure winners or sure losers" and "Whatley has been a sure loser throughout 2026, running as Donald Trump’s ‘guy,’ and making zero effort to build his own brand." "All Whatley had to do was to keep this race competitive, but instead the party is facing a potential wipeout. This is an embarrassing effort by a former RNC chairman who only has himself and his consultants to blame for the completely avoidable beat down coming on Nov. 3," the person added. Spokespeople for Tillis did not respond to a request for comment. Whatley's campaign declined to comment. Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, touted the president’s endorsement record in a statement. More pointedly, she said that “Republicans who chose not to help elect other Republicans may as well be helping Democrats.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment. While the dynamic is less pronounced on the House side — Reps. Don Bacon and Elise Stefanik have been helpful to the Republicans running to replace them — there’s a clear exception: Amodei. Flippo, who’s trying to replace him, has dealt with a host of scandals, from stolen valor accusations to carpetbagging to campaign finance issues , but Trump’s endorsement helped boost him through the Republican primary in June . Top Republican outside groups, including Club for Growth, have poured millions into his race in Nevada’s 2nd District to rescue a seat the president won by 14 points in 2024. Amodei said in an interview that whoever was advising Trump to jump in and endorse Flippo gave “awful advice.” "The only criteria shouldn't be, ‘Well, they're the Republican,’” said Amodei, who cast his ballot for a third-party candidate this week. “I mean, politics is a team sport. But when a member of the team turns out to be this way, clearly this is not a bright and shining moment for the vetting process." Asked about Club for Growth president McIntosh's criticism of moderate "bedwetting," Amodei scoffed: "At least this crowd is absolutely consistent. Forget fundamental factual and character messes that campaigns won't and can't respond to; and attempt to change the focus to party loyalty," the retiring representative said. "Let me know when Club For Growth does a statement on campaign finance compliance, stolen Valor, and individual background transparency.” Even as figures like Cornyn and Amodei catch the fury of more Trump-aligned Republican forces for not falling behind the party line, that doesn't mean they’re abandoning fellow Republicans overall. Cornyn has raised more than $1.1 million at events in Dallas and Houston last month for the campaigns of Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Jon Husted of Ohio and Dan Sullivan of Alaska — as well as for the National Republican Senatorial Committee and other Senate candidates: Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson, former Michigan Rep. Mike Rogers and former New Hampshire Sen. John Sununu, according to a person familiar with the senator’s political operation who was granted anonymity to discuss private events. He still clearly and explicitly draws a line against helping Paxton, telling reporters earlier this year, “Everything I said about him in the primary is true.” A spokesperson for Paxton did not respond to a request for comment. In Georgia, popular GOP Gov. Brian Kemp has been all-in on the governor’s race for Republican Rick Jackson — but he’s been comparatively quieter when it comes to Rep. Mike Collins’ Senate campaign to oust Democrat Jon Ossoff. The governor had initially recruited, backed and supported a different candidate in the GOP primary, though he’s since helped the Collins campaign with a public endorsement and by headlining a major fundraiser in Atlanta and others. Still, some Collins allies want the governor to be more involved. “Brian Kemp is someone who needs to be on the trail and someone who needs to help if Republicans are going to win,” said one GOP strategist working on races in Georgia who supports Collins and was granted anonymity to discuss internal dynamics. “But he did create some of this mess with the primary he ran against Mike who we all knew would be the nominee.” Meyer Sigfried, a Collins spokesperson, in a statement dismissed any suggestion that Kemp isn’t fully supporting Collins: “He’s been on the trail rallying Georgians to get out and vote early for Mike and Republicans up and down the ballot, and his help behind the scenes has been just as important.” A representative for Kemp referred POLITICO to Collins’ statement of support. Across the map, other frustrated Republicans have more directly pointed the finger at Trump for his interference, lambasting the president’s tendency to prop up candidates whom they deem too weak for the role. In South Carolina, Rep. Ralph Norman said this week he has refused to campaign with Sen. Darline Graham, who defeated him in the primary with Trump’s help. Graham has been under scrutiny for her lack of experience in elected office. Republicans still expect her to win in deep-red South Carolina, but they’ve also made late investments to shore up her campaign as Democrat Annie Andrews dominates in fundraising. Norman blamed the president , saying, "What he did to South Carolina … it's just not right,” but added he will still vote for Graham. T.W. Arrighi, a spokesperson for Graham, thanked the representative for his support in a statement, before hammering other Republicans — like Norman’s son, Warren Norman — who will not be voting for the GOP nominee: “It is unconscionable for anyone who claims to be a conservative in South Carolina to not vote straight ticket Republican and therefore endorse a Chuck Schumer-led Senate.” In many cases, GOP lawmakers are defending their disgruntled colleagues who have decided not to help Trump-picked candidates. "Folks have to follow their conscience. If a guy 'smells bad' then I wouldn’t,” said Bacon, who is supporting Brinker Harding, an Omaha city councilmember, in the race to replace him in his blue-leaning Nebraska district. "I like Brinker. He’s a good person."A “I believe we all ought to do all we can to help the good guys win the election,” Cramer added. “But I also understand people that ... feel aggrieved and want to maybe not be as enthusiastic about that as I am.” Mia McCarthy, Meredith Lee Hill and Aaron Pellish contributed to this report.
articles.headline: Spurned by Trump, these outgoing Republicans aren’t helping their potential successors

articles.body: Republican Ashley Hinson wants Iowans to know she’ll pick a fight with President Donald Trump. Democrat Josh Turek wants them to know he’ll work with him. The rivals in Iowa’s closely contested Senate race each sought to establish their independence in separate interviews aired Sunday on ABC’s “This Week,” pitching themselves as willing to put their state ahead of their respective party loyalty. Asked about her campaign pledge to be Trump’s “strongest ally” in the Senate, Hinson added a condition: “If it’s for Iowa.” “I will be someone’s ally when they’re with me on the issues that are important to Iowa,” the Republican lawmaker said. “And if they’re wrong, I’m going to pick a fight with them, no matter who that is.” The conflicting comments come in a state Trump won by 13 points in the 2024 presidential election, but where Democrats now see an opportunity to win their first Senate election since 2008. The president campaigned in Iowa this past week as high fuel costs and frustration with his tariffs complicate Republicans’ efforts to maintain the seat. Republicans close to Hinson told POLITICO last month that she needed to put some distance between herself and Trump, warning that his tariff agenda and the Iran war were undermining her chances. On Sunday, Hinson rejected Trump’s positive assessment of the economy. “Well, sure doesn’t feel like it right now,” she said, later criticizing the administration’s dealings with Moscow. “I don’t think we should be making any deals with Russia,” she said, pointing to her vote for sanctions. Her campaign told POLITICO on Friday that she opposed sanctions relief for Russia while supporting Trump’s use of the Defense Production Act to bolster domestic energy production. But there were limits to her criticism. While calling for the Iran war to end quickly, Hinson declined to oppose a potential new offensive after the midterms, saying she trusted Trump and the military to determine what needed to be done. Turek, meanwhile, called himself a “proud moderate” and sidestepped a question about whether Democrats had moved too far left. “I don’t think a lot about the party as a whole. I think about myself, and I think about Iowa,” the Democratic state representative said. That pitch follows a primary victory aided by national Democratic support , including from Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s leadership PAC — which contributed the maximum to Turek’s campaign, though Schumer did not formally endorse. VoteVets spent more than $10 million advertising on Turek’s behalf. He’s also secured the formal endorsement of former President Barack Obama, who appeared in an ad alongside Turek as the two played basketball. Asked what Trump had done right, Turek said Trump had done “a better job on the border than Biden, for sure.” He also cited agreement on keeping private equity out of housing and eliminating taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security, while arguing that Trump’s economic policies had concentrated wealth and power. Also asked whether endorsements mattered, Turek offered a blunt assessment: “Probably not.”
articles.headline: Iowa’s Senate rivals pitch independence from their parties

articles.body: AI chatbots are feeding non-native English speakers inaccurate information about the election, community activists and researchers warn, creating a barrier for some voters ahead of the midterms. The challenge — which leading AI companies say they’re working to address — is distinct from intentional disinformation campaigns that have plagued the internet for decades. Instead, some researchers and community leaders warn that voters prompting chatbots in non-English languages are unintentionally being fed inaccurate and ambiguous information — like whether they can vote by mail in their state — or overly literal translations that confuse electoral terms and lack context in various languages’ unique dialects. But the end result, the activists said, could still be the same: Voters whose native language is not English are more vulnerable to incorrect information and excluded from the most reliable answers ahead of the midterms. “Latino communities cannot afford to be left behind as artificial intelligence transforms how people work, learn, communicate and access information,” said Héctor Sánchez Barba, the president and CEO of Mi Familia Vota. “The history of the immigrant community and the Latino community has been one where we have been historically and structurally excluded from the best technology and access to information.” This digital divide has arisen, the activists and researchers say, in large part because AI models are trained in English, and fail to capture the nuances of other languages. Experts and grassroots organizations say this discrepancy in accuracy unintentionally disenfranchises non-English speaking voters across the country, where more than 20% of Americans speak a language other than English at home. National voter organizations that work in Latino and Asian American communities are grappling with how to bridge the gap and keep up with the rapidly developing technology to ensure that their communities don’t get left behind. Mi Familia Vota, which oversees some of the largest Latino voter mobilization efforts in the country, has built its own AI assistant dubbed “Nubi,” which comes from la nube or cloud in Spanish, for Spanish speakers seeking information on voting, voter registration and citizenship. The model is trained on government and nonpartisan datasets — as well as community data collected over 30 years of canvassing, town halls and citizenship workshops, said Denise Cook, chief innovation officer of Mi Familia Vota. She said it includes dialects of Mexican, Central American, South American and Caribbean Spanish, which have different words for election-related terminology. Polling place, for example, can be referred to as casilla , recinto or colegio electoral depending on the dialect, she said. Christine Choi, director of strategic communications at APIAVote, a civic engagement group for Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders, added that if AI fails to capture cultural and political nuances, “you can alienate a whole community or turn them off if you use the wrong interpretation.” A study by the Institute of Strategic Dialogue released in September found that accuracy of AI chatbots declined 16% when prompted in Spanish about voter information. Spanish prompts were more likely to produce incomplete or ambiguous answers, omitting relevant details and relying on overly literal translations, said Valeria de la Fuente Suárez, the lead author of the ISD study. “When voters are asking about registration deadlines or ID requirements, missing details can have real consequences,” she said. “Spanish-speaking voters deserve the same standards of clear, reliable and properly sourced information as English-speaking voters.” The study tested six frontier models through their respective APIs, or application programming interfaces, which are available for other developers to use. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google said in separate statements that they were working to refine their models for non-English languages, but APIs are not appropriate representations of how consumers interact with the actual chatbot interfaces, because they often include other fail-safes like popups or banners linking to external sources of information on voting. "Gemini is designed to respond with accurate and timely information and performed well in this analysis,” David Thompson, a spokesperson for Google, said in a statement. “However, this report accessed Gemini through our developer API, not the Gemini App, which has different protections and is how most people use our AI." Still, the leading AI companies say they are working to better provide election-related information to a wider swath of voters. To improve election information ahead of the midterms, OpenAI and Anthropic both said they are integrating information from Democracy Works , a nonprofit that collects official election information from the government, in its answers. “OpenAI's goal is to support people’s ability to participate freely in elections and make their own decisions with reliable information, transparency, and effective safeguards,” Nate Evans, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said in a statement. Some groups like Asian Texans for Justice, a nonprofit that works to increase voter engagement in Asian American communities in the battleground state, have opted to steer clear of the technology ahead of the midterms. “I do know that AI is being used more and more by AAPI communities, and we have made an organizational decision not to use AI for our in-language outreach due to inaccuracies,” said Nabila Mansoor, executive director of the organization. Spanish, Chinese and Vietnamese are among the most widely spoken languages in the U.S. besides English, but there are more than 500 other languages and language groups spoken across the country, according to the U.S. Census Bureau . The vast majority are considered low-resource languages with limited digitized data to train AI models, including Arabic, which has 1.3 million speakers in the U.S., and Swahili, which has about 150,000 speakers. And leading tech companies say they will try to address language-related access to AI systems more broadly. The Gates Foundation announced in September a coalition of 60 companies including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google dedicated to improving AI tools for an estimated 3.4 billion people around the world who speak languages underrepresented in AI models over the next five years. The joint commitment said, “The barrier is no longer the technology, which will only continue to improve. It requires a decision — to treat the world's languages as a shared foundation worth building, together, for everyone.” Community organizers say that while they welcome industry efforts to improve, the changes need to happen as soon as possible so immigrant communities can be equipped with the most reliable information for not only the midterms but the presidential election in 2028. “The way people get information has fundamentally changed and civic engagement has to change with it,” said Mi Familia Vota’s Barba.
articles.headline: AI has a language gap. That could be a problem for some voters.

articles.body: SYDNEY — Former Prime Minister John Howard urged the Australian government to reverse its plans to sell defense land in prime locations at a rally Sunday characterized by multipartisan bonhomie on-stage — and angry calls for Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to resign off stage. Howard told a crowd of a few thousand gathered in Sydney near the site of its Victoria Barracks that he would be the first to congratulate Albanese if he changed course on the land selloff. Also present at the rally were members of the nationalist One Nation party. Orange shirt-clad members of the far-right party and others wearing blue Make Albo Go Away (MAGA) hats called instead for Albanese to resign or be sacked. Decades of local opposition to higher density, often characterized by not-in-my-backyard politics, has left Sydney with one of the most expensive housing markets in the world. Most mainstream political parties have responded, now declaring themselves "YIMBY." The defense land selloff is one exception to this pendulum reversal, uniting groups across the political spectrum. Few things unite Australia like its Australia and New Zealand Army Corps legend, the belief that the values embodied by its armed forces, such as mateship, are central to its national character. So the decision by the Albanese government to sell Department of Defense assets around the country, including prime harbor-front properties in Sydney, to raise 3 billion Australian dollars (in gross terms), or 1.8 billion (net), may seem like a strange one. With calls to reduce the deficit and the need to find land for housing in Australia’s sprawling cities, the government thought it was on firm footing disposing of properties it says are surplus to requirements. Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles has argued his Department of Defense is not best placed to preserve the heritage value of the sites, and that money for their upkeep would be better spent on future fighting capability. The selloff proposal has met fierce resistance across parties: from the conservative Liberal-National Coalition, the traditional opposition in Australia; right-wing nationalist One Nation; the left-wing Greens; and even members of Albanese’s own party, his Labor colleagues in the NSW state government. The Albanese government has been urged by its opponents to spend less to lower inflation and prevent the need for further interest rate hikes. But many savings measures have been blocked: from its attempts to make the private health insurance rebate and veterans’ allied health entitlements less generous, to charging residents of aged care more for services. Howard, a conservative Liberal, told the crowd he is “all in favor of governments spending less and taxing less” but that was not the issue at hand. “What is more important to the soul of a nation? [Than] its history, its heritage, and those that have gone before,” he said. “You don’t give that up for a few bob.” Howard’s speech veered from his memories of seeing Australian cricket legend Don Bradman bat at the nearby Sydney Cricket Ground, to Victoria Barracks’ history as the departure point for soldiers bound for the 1885 Sudan War, to his description of the 28-degree Celsius day — 4.3 degrees above the historical late-October average — as “seasonably warm.” Tony Abbott, another former Prime Minister and now the Liberal Party president tasked with combating the rise of One Nation, said it was “wonderful” to gather with Australians who respect its history and heritage. “And isn’t it wonderful to be at this protest, where the only flag on display is the Australian flag — and not the Palestinian one.” Labor’s NSW parliamentary secretary for transport, Marjorie O’Neill, one of the protest organizers, was jeered by the One Nation-heavy crowd: first, for beginning the rally with an acknowledgment of country for Australia’s First Nations people and for 150 Aboriginal men who had signed up to serve the defense forces at Victoria Barracks; and then again for omitting mention of One Nation as she credited the multilateral coalition of Labor, Liberal and Greens against the sale. Liberal senator Jess Collins, her co-organizer, added “I will acknowledge that we do have One Nation here too” — to loud cheers. Independent MP Allegra Spender urged the crowd to join a convoy to Canberra being organized for Nov. 23 to protest the sale. One Nation members approached ahead of the rally declined to comment, due to party rules forbidding speaking to the media. Justin Bowra, a member of the Greens and local resident, told POLITICO that “despite all the political colours, whether you’re orange, blue, red or green, we all agree on one thing: The wrong thing to do is sell off the land to the highest bidder for private development.” “The right thing to do is let the community decide, let locals decide, and make those decisions with the benefit of all Australians in mind rather than turning them into a bunch of condos.” The NSW Government, led by Labor’s Chris Minns, has also opposed the sale, but has no constitutional power to stop it, leaving the ball in Albanese and Marles’ court. Abbott told the rally that “people power” will prevail. Former Army chief Lt. Gen. Ken Gillespie told the rally that with politically motivated violence on the rise in Australia, including the Bondi antisemitic terror attack of Dec. 14, 2025, it was important to retain the barracks, which is used for counter-terrorism exercises by the Special Air Service. “When police need military support in a crisis, minutes matter,” he said. Marles angered many by previously dismissing those campaigning against the sale as “a few former generals who liked hanging out there.” The description appears particularly inapt now — a poor read on the practical difficulty of opposing so many political interests simultaneously, and an underestimation of the potent symbolism of the ANZAC legend.
articles.headline: Australian defense land selloff runs into multiparty opposition

articles.body: Former Rep. Mary Peltola is postponing campaign stops in her bid for Alaska’s Senate seat after she and her family sustained minor injuries in a car crash Saturday night. Peltola and her family were traveling to the Alaska Federation of Natives’ annual banquet when another driver struck their vehicle, her campaign announced Sunday on social media. “Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits,” campaign manager Cheryl Bruce said in the statement. “Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary’s upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover.” Anchorage police said a vehicle rear-ended the car carrying Peltola at a red light Saturday evening, pushing it into a third vehicle. Peltola and the other passengers of her car were taken to a local hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, police said. The driver who struck their vehicle was also hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries. Police said the crash remains under investigation. The crash disrupts the start of Peltola’s eight-community “Alaska Always Tour,” a seven-day campaign swing ahead of the midterms. Events in Fairbanks and Bethel originally scheduled for Sunday and Monday will be rescheduled, while stops in Homer, Kenai, Seward, Juneau, Anchorage and Palmer will continue as planned, the campaign said. The midterm elections are just over a week away. Peltola, a Democrat, is challenging Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in a closely watched race that could help determine control of the Senate. The race on Thursday became the subject of a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of the election results if Sullivan loses in November. The administration is arguing that the presence of an independent candidate also named Dan Sullivan is an effort to mislead voters, despite the Alaska Supreme Court allowing the other Sullivan to remain on the ballot in a June ruling. Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the lawsuit Sunday, arguing that voters could confuse the two candidates. Peltola’s campaign called the suit a “despicable political threat to overturn the election.” Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) piled on, saying the Justice Department's suit should never have been filed. Alaska’s political history has been marked by fatal transportation disasters. Peltola’s husband, Eugene “Buzzy” Peltola Jr., died in September 2023 when the small plane he was piloting crashed after takeoff in southwestern Alaska. Former Republican Sen. Ted Stevens died in a plane crash in 2010 near Dillingham, and Democratic Rep. Nick Begich disappeared in 1972 after disembarking from Anchorage on a small plane traveling to Juneau.
articles.headline: Peltola postpones campaign stops after Saturday car crash

articles.body: <p>El PP no va a dejar pasar los disturbios del fin de semana pasado en Barcelona, cuando un grupo de jóvenes vandalizaron y robaron en 23 comercios y provocaron 33 incendios convocados a través de las redes sociales. <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/catalunya/2026-10-24/centenares-de-jovenes-violentos-destrozan-el-centro-de-barcelona.html" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/catalunya/2026-10-24/centenares-de-jovenes-violentos-destrozan-el-centro-de-barcelona.html">La policía detuvo a 128 personas</a>, de las cuales más de la mitad son menores de edad, y todavía se desconoce quién está detrás de la convocatoria. Génova da el máximo relieve a estos incidentes, hasta el punto de que Alberto Núñez Feijóo va a convertirlos en un eje de su campaña en el corto plazo, según avanzan fuentes de la dirección popular. articles.body: <img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/PKPVM35DRVAIRCVX7QPV6TNAJA.jpg?auth=5d5b47a8549f90f165247c97bf61437f6a2df235527979278e9f343a1b213610" width="3648" height="2432" alt="Abdellah Mustafa, a finales de agosto en el campamento de mujeres de Sidi Embarek. "></img><p>Se apellida Mustafa, pero es casi decorativo. Según el Instituto Nacional de Estadística hay otros 60 Abdellah en Ceuta, y si alguien necesita precisar que se refieren a él, bastan dos palabras a las que está indisolublemente unido: <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-14/el-gobierno-se-ocupara-del-campamento-de-sidi-embarek-el-cobijo-de-300-mujeres-y-ninos-que-levanto-la-solidaridad-de-ceuta.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-14/el-gobierno-se-ocupara-del-campamento-de-sidi-embarek-el-cobijo-de-300-mujeres-y-ninos-que-levanto-la-solidaridad-de-ceuta.html">Sidi Embarek</a>. Su barrio, en la periferia ceutí, del que es presidente vecinal desde 2022, donde levantó el campamento solidario de mujeres y niñas más grande tras el cruce masivo de migrantes. Ahora Abdellah recupera de cierta manera su apellido, porque así es como figurará en las papeletas como candidato al Senado por Ceuta en las próximas elecciones del 29-N. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-27/abdellah-mustafa-de-cocinero-a-candidato-al-senado-por-ceuta.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p><img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/BRWRN3PEBVCAVBPJ5D6IUCYFIY.jpg?auth=9a27398cb04aa1fbd71c5757c51783d7655f5629d4522c5a37fb9c0064255a5d" width="6000" height="4000" alt="Karima Mustafa, la coordinadora del campamento de mujeres de Sidi Embarek, en Ceuta, el 9 de septiembre de 2026. "></img>

articles.body: <p>Los camellos que rodean a la jaima de Muamar El Gadafi en Trípoli (Libia) son solo un espejismo. “Dios mío”, exclama José María Aznar, entonces presidente del Gobierno (1996-2004), cuando ve a Najar el Jayed, <i>El Rayo del Líder, </i>un purasangre enjaezado que le acaba de regalar Gadafi (<a href="https://elpais.com/diario/2003/09/19/espana/1063922415_850215.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/diario/2003/09/19/espana/1063922415_850215.html">2003</a>). El caballo acaba en España, como ocurre años después con la silla de montar con la que Gadafi agasaja a <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-06-18/un-reloj-con-esmeraldas-figuras-de-oro-y-plata-o-una-botella-de-vodka-los-500-regalos-que-declaro-zapatero-como-presidente.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-06-18/un-reloj-con-esmeraldas-figuras-de-oro-y-plata-o-una-botella-de-vodka-los-500-regalos-que-declaro-zapatero-como-presidente.html">José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero (2004-2011)</a>. El listado de los obsequios recibidos por el expresidente socialista está ahora en el centro de la polémica: el <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-23/el-juez-pide-a-patrimonio-que-aclare-los-regalos-a-presidencia-del-gobierno-de-2004-a-2011-para-aclarar-el-origen-de-las-joyas-de-zapatero.html" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-23/el-juez-pide-a-patrimonio-que-aclare-los-regalos-a-presidencia-del-gobierno-de-2004-a-2011-para-aclarar-el-origen-de-las-joyas-de-zapatero.html">magistrado José Luis Calama</a> ha solicitado a Patrimonio Nacional que le remita el inventario completo tras encontrar joyas en la caja fuerte del despacho del exlíder del PSOE durante la investigación del <i>caso Plus Ultra. </i>Zapatero las atribuye a un obsequio personal del <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-23/estas-son-las-12-joyas-que-zapatero-senala-como-un-regalo-del-rey-saudi-en-2007.html" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-23/estas-son-las-12-joyas-que-zapatero-senala-como-un-regalo-del-rey-saudi-en-2007.html">monarca saudí Abdalá Bin Abdulaziz Al-Saud</a>. Pero el registro oficial de los regalos recibidos por los expresidentes del siglo XXI, al que accedió este diario en aplicación de la ley de transparencia, no las recoge. En contraste, sí muestra una mezcla de objetos de lujo y diseñados para sorprender o para retratar una época. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-27/un-sombrero-cowboy-para-aznar-un-ladrillo-de-una-carcel-para-zapatero-y-un-boli-bala-para-rajoy-los-sorprendentes-regalos-a-los-presidentes.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: Un sombrero cowboy para Aznar, un ladrillo de una cárcel para Zapatero y un boli bala para Rajoy: los sorprendentes regalos a los presidentes

articles.body: <p>Cuando ETA anunció, el 20 de octubre de 2011, el “cese definitivo” de la violencia terrorista, 703 de sus miembros estaban encarcelados. <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-20/quince-anos-despues-el-final-del-terrorismo-etarra-sigue-sin-reconocerse.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-20/quince-anos-despues-el-final-del-terrorismo-etarra-sigue-sin-reconocerse.html">Tres lustros después</a>, ese número se ha reducido a 110 presos etarras ―un 85% menos― tras la salida de la cárcel el pasado 13 de octubre de Roberto Lebrero Panizo, el último hasta ahora en quedar en libertad. Un acusado descenso del número de reclusos que, sin embargo, refleja solo una parte de la profunda transformación que ha vivido este colectivo desde que la organización terrorista anunció que <a href="https://elpais.com/especiales/2017/desarme-definitivo-de-eta/" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/especiales/2017/desarme-definitivo-de-eta/">abandonaba las armas</a>.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-27/de-703-a-110-presos-en-15-anos-asi-se-ha-transformado-eta-en-las-carceles.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: De 703 a 110 presos en 15 años: así se ha transformado ETA en las cárceles

articles.body: <p>Lo que parecía imposible <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones/generales/" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones/generales/">en la campaña de las últimas elecciones generales</a>, cuando el PP se esforzó en mantener distancias con Vox, ha sucedido ahora, en la batalla decisiva del 29 de noviembre. Los populares han alcanzado un acuerdo con la extrema derecha para concurrir de forma estratégica al Senado, en lo que supone una coalición de facto, para evitar que se pierdan escaños de la derecha allí donde los de Santiago Abascal tenían muy difícil lograr representación. En virtud del acuerdo, que han anunciado a la vez PP y Vox esta mañana, los dos partidos coordinan un total de 31 circunscripciones. Los populares renuncian a presentarse en tres provincias (Gipuzkoa, Girona y Tarragona), mientras que Vox no se presentará en otras seis provincias (Cádiz, Valencia, Castellón, Las Palmas, Santa Cruz de Tenerife y Baleares). Lo que ocurre que, en el caso de las islas, las provincias se dividen en varias circunscripciones (Gran Canaria, Tenerife, El Hierro, Fuerteventura, Lanzarote, La Palma y La Gomera, Mallorca, Menorca, Ibiza y Formentera—). Así que, los ultras se retiran de seis provincias, que suman 14 circunscripciones.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-26/la-derecha-pacta-sus-candidaturas-en-el-senado-pp-se-retira-en-gipuzkoa-girona-y-tarragona-y-vox-en-otras-seis-provincias.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: La derecha pacta sus candidaturas en el Senado: el PP se retira en Gipuzkoa, Girona y Tarragona y Vox en otras seis provincias

articles.body: <p>El Partido Popular y Vox han anunciado este lunes un acuerdo estratégico para las listas al Senado en 23 provincias para las elecciones del 29-N. Los de Santiago Abascal no se presentarán en seis provincias y el PP retira su candidatura de tres territorios. Además, Vox solo presentará un candidato en otras 14 provincias. El secretario general popular, Miguel Tellado, ha calificado el acuerdo de “buena noticia para el PP, para la alternancia a [Pedro] Sánchez y para España”. Por su parte, el secretario general de Vox, Ignacio Garriga, ha calificado de “útil” el acuerdo, y ha subrayado que, pese a que el PP y Vox son “partidos muy diferentes”, coinciden “en la necesidad de expulsar a Sánchez”. Tellado ha asegurado en una rueda de prensa que <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-23/feijoo-intentara-gobernar-aunque-no-sea-la-lista-mas-votada-mi-primer-objetivo-es-que-sanchez-se-vaya.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-23/feijoo-intentara-gobernar-aunque-no-sea-la-lista-mas-votada-mi-primer-objetivo-es-que-sanchez-se-vaya.html">el objetivo es “proteger la mayoría del centro derecha en el Senado</a> frente a los movimientos de la izquierda radical para arrebatársela”. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-26/claves-del-acuerdo-entre-el-pp-y-vox-para-las-listas-del-senado-donde-cede-abascalen-que-provincias-se-retira-feijoo.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: Claves del acuerdo entre el PP y Vox para las listas del Senado: ¿dónde cede Abascal?, ¿en qué provincias se retira Feijóo?

articles.body: <img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/4HWF6XYB6JD4RKQFOHHXIIKZ4M.JPG?auth=a171fe1c0bf34f376d17a2680f24d4631c3b5370db69005cc7adbe6cd6cd9654" width="4016" height="2678" alt="El presidente del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, durante la clausura del mitin que esta formación ha celebrado este viernes en el Palau de les Arts de Valencia."></img><p>Alberto Núñez Feijóo se rodea de varios vicesecretarios, miembros de su dirección y de su equipo directo <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-22/alvarez-de-toledo-y-semper-seran-los-numeros-dos-y-tres-de-feijoo-en-la-lista-por-madrid.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-22/alvarez-de-toledo-y-semper-seran-los-numeros-dos-y-tres-de-feijoo-en-la-lista-por-madrid.html">en la lista de Madrid para las próximas elecciones del 29 de noviembre</a>. Más allá de los puestos dos, tres y cuatro, que se hicieron públicos hace unos días, y que ocupan Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo, Borja Sémper y Alma Ezcurra, el líder del PP ha incluido en la candidatura que él mismo encabeza al Congreso a varios dirigentes destacados de su núcleo duro. Así, el vicesecretario de Educación e Igualdad, Jaime de los Santos, asciende al puesto cinco (desde el 12 en las anteriores), y el de Economía, Alberto Nadal, que no fue en las últimas, será el nueve. El secretario de Internacional de la dirección, el diplomático Ildefonso Castro, también se incorpora en el puesto 11. Además, la jefa de gabinete de Feijóo, Marta Varela, concurre como número seis, y la jefa de proyección e imagen, Mar Sánchez, en el ocho. Como novedad, Feijóo ha incluido también a la nueva responsable de Estrategia de la dirección popular, María Martín, en el puesto 12.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-26/jaime-de-los-santos-alberto-nadal-y-el-nucleo-duro-de-genova-acompanan-a-feijoo-en-la-lista-del-pp-por-madrid.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>Los regresos no voluntarios de migrantes de Ceuta a Marruecos empiezan a ejecutarse. El Gobierno devolvió el viernes a 16 personas llegadas con la entrada masiva a la ciudad autónoma, la mayoría de origen subsahariano. Las administraciones ordenaron su retorno tras denegarles la solicitud de protección internacional, según confirman fuentes del Ministerio de Interior. Este es un escenario distinto al de los “retornos voluntarios” que se venían produciendo en suelo ceutí desde hace semanas. En su caso, a los citados 16 migrantes, “se les denegó la protección internacional” tras culminar la tramitación de sus expedientes. Tenían plazo para recurrir, “pero no lo hicieron”. Y, cumplido ese plazo, se les retornó al país vecino, según las mismas fuentes.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-26/el-gobierno-empieza-a-devolver-migrantes-de-ceuta-con-expedientes-judiciales.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: El Gobierno retorna a Marruecos a migrantes de la entrada masiva de Ceuta tras denegarles la protección internacional

articles.body: <p>La ministra de Defensa, <a href="https://elpais.com/noticias/margarita-robles/" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/noticias/margarita-robles/">Margarita Robles</a>, ha subrayado este lunes en Naciones Unidas el papel de la mujer en la resolución de los conflictos y ha advertido de que “la paz no puede construirse de espaldas a la mitad de la humanidad”. Robles, que ha participado en el encuentro de alto nivel sobre mujeres, paz y seguridad celebrado en Nueva York, ha planteado un objetivo mínimo del 5% de participación femenina en las Fuerzas Armadas y por encima del 15% para los países “que ya cuentan con una presencia apreciable de mujeres” en sus ejércitos (<a href="https://elpais.com/noticias/mujeres-militares/" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/noticias/mujeres-militares/">en España representan el 13,4%</a>). Además, ha pedido aumentar hasta un porcentaje de entre el 13% y el 15% su participación en misiones militares de la ONU —las mujeres suponen el 10.6% de los contingentes españoles en el exterior— y crear, como estímulo, un distintivo o reconocimiento para las militares que acumulen tiempo de servicio en operaciones de paz. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-26/robles-advierte-en-la-onu-de-que-la-paz-no-puede-construirse-de-espaldas-a-las-mujeres.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

El mando del instituto armado, que se encontraba desplegado en la frontera en labores operativas, <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-07/la-audiencia-nacional-asume-la-investigacion-sobre-la-entrada-masiva-de-ceuta-por-atacar-gravemente-la-integralidad-territorial-de-espana.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-07/la-audiencia-nacional-asume-la-investigacion-sobre-la-entrada-masiva-de-ceuta-por-atacar-gravemente-la-integralidad-territorial-de-espana.html">ha subrayado a la jueza María Tardón</a> que él tomó esa decisión por iniciativa propia —sin recibir órdenes de sus superiores o de la Delegación del Gobierno— después de que agentes de la Policía Nacional “se pusieran” a intentar “parar el flujo” de personas y se generara, según ha considerado, la posibilidad de que se provocase “un aplastamiento”.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-26/un-mando-de-la-guardia-civil-de-ceuta-explica-que-se-mantuvo-abierta-una-puerta-de-la-valla-por-riesgo-de-tapon-humano-en-la-entrada-masiva.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
